section_title: Why does God choose the son still out with the sheep?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Now the LORD said to Samuel, “How long are you going to mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself.” 2 “How can I go?” Samuel asked. “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” The LORD answered, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.’ 3 Then invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you are to do. You are to anoint for Me the one I indicate.” 4 So Samuel did what the LORD had said and went to Bethlehem. When the elders of the town met him, they trembled and asked, “Do you come in peace?” 5 “In peace,” he replied. “I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” Then he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.

6 When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and said, “Surely here before the LORD is His anointed.” 7 But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him; the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” 8 Then Jesse called Abinadab and presented him to Samuel, who said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.” 9 Next Jesse presented Shammah, but Samuel said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.” 10 Thus Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel told him, “The LORD has not chosen any of these.”

11 And Samuel asked him, “Are these all the sons you have?” “There is still the youngest,” Jesse replied, “but he is tending the sheep.” “Send for him,” Samuel replied. “For we will not sit down to eat until he arrives.” 12 So Jesse sent for his youngest son and brought him in. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. And the LORD said, “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one.” 13 So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the presence of his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. Then Samuel set out and went to Ramah.

context_lines: Samuel is still mourning Saul when the LORD sends him to Jesse’s family in Bethlehem. God has chosen a king from among Jesse’s sons. Samuel fears Saul will kill him if he hears, so God directs him to take a heifer and hold a sacrifice. The visit has a real purpose of worship as well as the appointment God will reveal.

The elders of Bethlehem meet Samuel with fear, but he assures them he comes in peace. Jesse and his sons are prepared for the sacrifice. When Samuel sees Eliab, he thinks he has found the chosen man. God corrects him: appearance and height do not reveal what God sees in the heart.

Seven sons pass before Samuel without being chosen. Only then does Samuel ask whether another remains. The youngest is tending sheep. The gathering waits while he is brought, and the LORD identifies him as the one to anoint.

David is himself described as handsome, with beautiful eyes. The point is that looks do not determine God’s choice, rather than that attractiveness disqualifies someone. Samuel anoints him before his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him. He has been chosen and equipped, but he does not take Saul’s throne that day.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/16.htm) emphasizes Samuel’s need to learn the lesson he had already seen with Saul: an impressive appearance cannot reveal a person’s heart. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/16.htm) likewise contrasts what people can see with the character God knows. The passage challenges a judgment based on appearance, while leaving God’s knowledge greater than ours.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) distinguishes David’s designation for kingship from his later accession. The anointing supplies a real calling and the Spirit’s gifts before his outward circumstances have become royal. The youngest son is still known as a shepherd even after God has chosen him.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/16.htm) reads David as a foreshadowing of Christ, God’s beloved Son. That wider Christian reading is not a claim that David will never sin. It recognizes God beginning a royal story whose full hope extends beyond the young man standing before Samuel.
god_plan_lines: David’s place and work form a well-supported connection with the coming shepherd-king. [Matthew 2:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/2.htm) identifies Bethlehem as Jesus’ birthplace and cites the promised ruler who will shepherd Israel. The same town that introduces Jesse’s shepherd son becomes the setting for the birth of the Messiah.

In [John 10:11–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/10.htm), Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd, knows His sheep and gives His life for them. David’s shepherding helps us understand the picture of care, but Jesus carries it further through His willing death and authority to take up His life again. The connection points toward a king whose rule serves and rescues His people.
